CausalChain: Chronic alcohol intake → Increased acetaldehyde production → Epigenetic modifications in intestinal epithelial cells → MicroRNA dysregulation → Downregulation of tight junction proteins (e.g., occludin, claudins) → Increased gut permeability → Enhanced endotoxin (LPS) translocation → Activation of Kupffer cells → Secretion of IL-6 and TNF-α → Activation of hepatic stellate cells via IL-6/STAT3 signaling → Accelerated liver fibrosis → Increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma
Hypothesis: Alcohol-induced epigenetic deregulation of gut epithelial microRNAs disrupts tight junction integrity, thereby increasing gut permeability and endotoxin translocation; this drives liver inflammation and stellate cell activation, especially when compounded by metabolic stress and genetic predispositions, ultimately promoting fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis in alcohol-associated liver disease.
Abstract: Chronic alcohol consumption is known to interfere with gut barrier function and promote liver disease via mechanisms including direct hepatocellular injury, inflammatory cytokine production and genetic predispositions. Building on current evidence, our novel hypothesis proposes that alcohol‐mediated epigenetic alterations—especially the dysregulation of gut epithelial microRNAs—may impair the expression of tight junction proteins. This in turn enhances intestinal permeability and facilitates an increased translocation of endotoxins into the portal circulation. Once in the liver, these endotoxins activate resident macrophages leading to production of pro‐inflammatory cytokines and activation of hepatic stellate cells through pathways such as IL‑6/STAT3. Furthermore, this process could synergize with metabolic stress factors such as obesity and predisposing PNPLA3 variants to accelerate liver fibrosis and promote hepatocarcinogenesis. This model suggests that targeting microRNA regulatory networks in the gut epithelium may represent a novel therapeutic avenue to prevent progression of alcohol‐associated liver disease to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
